screens.title: Event Monitoring and Advanced On-Chain Interactions
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore how smart contracts communicate with the off-chain world using events, and why this matters for responsive dApps. Events are structured logs emitted by contracts that off-chain services read efficiently. You will learn the Solidity syntax for defining and emitting events, the role of the indexed keyword for fast filtering, and how listeners in ethers. js subscribe to live events. We will also cover how to extract event data from a transaction receipt after a transaction is mined, and contrast that with live listening. Finally, we examine advanced interaction patterns such as batching multiple actions and consciously setting gas parameters for time-sensitive operations. Throughout the lesson you'll see concrete code examples: a modified Counter contract that emits CountChanged events, a Hardhat listener script that prints events as they arrive, and examples of queryFilter and parseLog usage to retrieve historical events or decode logs. By the end you'll understand when to use events instead of storing history on-chain, how to filter efficiently, and how to handle receipts and gas in real deployments.

screens.title: Solidity Events: Syntax and 'indexed'
screens.narratorSegment: Let's define what a Solidity event is and how to author one correctly. Events are structured logs created by the EVM when a contract executes an emit statement. They are recorded in the transaction receipt and are intended for off-chain consumers, not on-chain logic. In Solidity you declare an event signature with the event keyword followed by parameter types and names. The indexed modifier can mark up to three parameters to be included in the searchable topics array. Indexed parameters make it possible for nodes and clients to filter large sets of logs efficiently, so choosing which fields to index matters in design. For example, a Transfer event often indexes the from and to addresses so dApps can quickly query transfers for a particular account. Keep in mind that indexing moves some data to topics, which affects how you parse logs. Emitting an event is done with emit EventName(args). Emitting costs gas but far less than persisting the same data in storage. A common misconception is that events are accessible to other contracts — they are not; events are for off-chain systems. As you write events, consider which arguments a frontend will want to filter by and mark those indexed. Try creating an event that balances searchability and argument completeness, and then ask: which two or three fields will you index and why?

keyIdea.title: Events vs storage
keyIdea.text: Use events to publish off-chain history; index the fields you will need to filter by to keep queries efficient.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Solidity Events
Event declaration and emit
Design decisions: which params to index and why.
// Solidity event example
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

contract Example {
  event Transfer(address indexed from, address indexed to, uint256 value);

  function send(address recipient, uint256 amount) public {
    // state updates here
    emit Transfer(msg.sender, recipient, amount);
  }
}
  • Indexed vs non-indexed: indexed fields are available as topics for efficient node-side filtering.
  • Gas trade-off: emitting events costs gas but considerably less than storage writes.
  • Off-chain target: events are read by UIs, backends, and analytics — not other contracts.
Key Takeaway

Choose indexed parameters for the fields you expect to filter by. Emit events for off-chain history instead of bulk storage.

Concrete example
Why index from/to in a transfer?
Scenario
A wallet UI needs to show recent transfers for a user address. If from and to are indexed, the UI can request only logs related to that address, avoiding scanning all Transfer logs.
Common mistake
Marking too many fields as indexed without need increases complexity and can mislead expectations of searchable data. Only index fields you will filter by.
Check your understanding
Name two fields you would index for a marketplace contract and explain why they help queries.

screens.title: Modify Counter.sol to emit CountChanged
screens.narratorSegment: Now we walk through modifying a simple Counter contract to emit a CountChanged event when the counter moves. The goal is to create a traceable history of user actions with minimal gas. Notice the event signature includes an indexed user address, the newCount, and a short action string to describe increment or decrement. Indexing the user address makes it easy to filter logs by who triggered the change. When writing the increment and decrement functions, increment or decrement the state variable and then emit CountChanged with msg. sender, the updated count, and a descriptive action. Keep the event arguments compact: strings are fine for short descriptors but avoid large blobs. A misconception to avoid is thinking events are part of contract state that other contracts can read — they are off-chain only. After updating the contract, redeploy to a test network and record the address; listeners and queryFilter calls must point at the new address. This simple event pattern is ideal for auditing user interactions, powering UI updates, and offloading historical data from storage. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Counter: Emit CountChanged
Updated Counter.sol
Keep event args minimal and index the user for filtering.
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

contract Counter {
  uint public count;

  event CountChanged(address indexed user, uint256 newCount, string action);

  constructor() {
    count = 0;
  }

  function increment() public {
    count++;
    emit CountChanged(msg.sender, count, "incremented");
  }

  function decrement() public {
    count--;
    emit CountChanged(msg.sender, count, "decremented");
  }
}
  • Index the address so UIs can query a specific user's changes quickly.
  • Keep the action string short; long strings increase log size unnecessarily.
  • Emit after state update so logs reflect the new state value.
Concrete example
After deploying, call increment from two accounts. A listener can show a live feed of who changed the counter and how.
Common mistake
Emitting events before updating state can confuse off-chain consumers about the actual stored value. Always update state then emit.
Pro tip
Use indexed for addresses or ids you will filter by; non-indexed fields carry the actual data payload.
Key Takeaway

Emit concise events after state changes. Index identity-like fields for fast queries.

The callback receives event arguments followed by an event object that contains the transaction hash and block number. Notice the example awaits nothing after attaching — the script keeps running to listen for new events. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Hardhat Listener
Listener script (Node / Hardhat)
Attach contract.on and keep the process alive for live updates.
// scripts/listen_events.js
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const CONTRACT_ADDRESS = "YOUR_NEWLY_DEPLOYED_COUNTER_ADDRESS"; // replace
  const CounterFactory = await ethers.getContractFactory("Counter");
  const counter = CounterFactory.attach(CONTRACT_ADDRESS);

  console.log(`Listening for CountChanged events on ${CONTRACT_ADDRESS}...`);

  counter.on("CountChanged", (user, newCount, action, event) => {
    console.log(`--- Event Detected ---`);
    console.log(`User: ${user}`);
    console.log(`New Count: ${newCount.toString()}`);
    console.log(`Action: ${action}`);
    console.log(`Transaction Hash: ${event.transactionHash}`);
    console.log(`Block Number: ${event.blockNumber}`);
    console.log(`----------------------`);
  });

  await new Promise(() => {});
}

main().catch((error) => {
  console.error(error);
  process.exitCode = 1;
});
  • Ensure the provider supports subscriptions (WebSocket) for near-real-time streaming.
  • In tests you can use HTTP polling providers with short intervals, but WebSockets are preferred for production listeners.
  • Attach error handling to reconnect on dropped connections in production services.
Terminal demo
Run the listener, then call increment in another terminal. The listener prints the event details including transaction hash and block number.
Listening for CountChanged events on 0xabc...123

--- Event Detected ---
User: 0xdef...456
New Count: 1
Action: incremented
Transaction Hash: 0xdeadbeef...
Block Number: 1234567
----------------------
Common mistake

Running the listener with an HTTP provider expecting push events will not deliver real-time results; verify provider capabilities first.

screens.title: Querying Historical Events with queryFilter
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond live listeners, you often need to reconstruct history or populate initial UI state by querying past events. ethers. js provides contract. queryFilter for that purpose. You can build a filter by event name or by using contract. filters. EventName(indexedParam,...). When parameters are indexed, you can pass a value to the filter so the node returns only matching logs in the specified block range. This is efficient because the node uses topics to restrict results. For example, to fetch all Minted events where owner equals a user address, create a filter with the user's address in the owner slot and call queryFilter with a start and end block. Always limit block ranges to reasonable sizes to avoid timeouts or huge responses. If you need a full history, paginate by block windows. A common misconception is that queryFilter returns decoded args for every log — it does decode known events for the contract ABI, but unrelated logs might throw when parsed. Wrap parse attempts in try-catch blocks when iterating over logs to safely skip unfamiliar entries. Querying Historical Events with queryFilter means use indexed filters with queryfilter and block ranges to get only the events you need without scanning all logs.. In practical terms, use filters and block ranges to reconstruct past activity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › queryFilter
Filter by indexed parameter
Use contract.filters to build efficient filters for queryFilter.
// Example: fetch Minted events for a specific owner
const userAddress = await signer.getAddress();
const filter = contract.filters.Minted(userAddress, null);
const mintedEvents = await contract.queryFilter(filter, startBlock, endBlock);
// mintedEvents now contains decoded event objects for this contract ABI
  • Always provide sensible start and end blocks to limit the scope.
  • Paginate over block windows for long histories to avoid timeouts.
  • If the ABI changes, be cautious: older logs may not decode cleanly.
Scenario
Build a UI list of NFTs minted by the connected user by filtering Minted events with the owner's address in the indexed slot.
Common mistake
Fetching all events and filtering client-side is inefficient and slow; prefer node-side filtering via indexed parameters where possible.
Key Takeaway

Use contract.filters with indexed fields and queryFilter over bounded block ranges to retrieve relevant historical logs efficiently.

screens.title: Parsing Transaction Receipts and Logs
screens.narratorSegment: When you send a transaction that changes state, you often want immediate confirmation that the contract emitted expected events. After awaiting tx. wait(), the TransactionReceipt contains a logs array with raw log objects. These logs include topics and data fields that correspond to event signatures and arguments. ethers. js exposes contract. interface. parseLog to decode a single log using the contract's ABI. Typical usage iterates receipt. logs and attempts to parse each log in a try-catch; logs that don't belong to your contract or unknown event signatures will throw and should be skipped. This approach is useful in tests and scripts where you want assertive validation that a specific event occurred with expected values. Remember that indexed parameters appear in topics and non-indexed args in data; parseLog handles decoding for you. A common error is assuming every log in the receipt will parse for your contract. Instead, guard parsing attempts and only inspect parsed. name and parsed. args when successful. Finally, parsing receipts is deterministic and immediate — ideal for confirmations and assertions following a state change. Parsing Transaction Receipts and Logs means iterate receipt.logs and safely parse with contract.interface.parselog to verify events emitted by a transaction.. In practical terms, use receipt.logs and contract.interface.parselog to decode events after tx.wait(). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Receipt parsing
keyIdea.text: Iterate receipt.logs and safely parse with contract.interface.parseLog to verify events emitted by a transaction.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Receipt Parsing
Parse logs from a receipt
Use parseLog to decode known event logs; skip unknown logs safely.
const tx = await contract.increment();
const receipt = await tx.wait();
for (const log of receipt.logs) {
  try {
    const parsed = contract.interface.parseLog(log);
    if (parsed.name === "CountChanged") {
      console.log(`Parsed event: ${parsed.args.user} -> ${parsed.args.newCount}`);
    }
  } catch (e) {
    // log not from this contract or unknown event — ignore
  }
}
  • Always use try-catch around parseLog to avoid crashing on unrelated logs.
  • Indexed fields live in topics; parseLog returns both indexed and non-indexed args in parsed.args.
  • Use this pattern in tests to assert the correct events were emitted with expected values.
Concrete example
After calling increment, a script can immediately confirm the user and newCount from the parsed receipt, providing a reliable assertion in tests and scripts.
Common mistake
Trying to parse logs without the correct contract interface will fail. Always attach the ABI for the contract you expect to parse.
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Advanced Interactions: Batching and Nonce Management
screens.narratorSegment: When building advanced workflows you may need to send multiple transactions in sequence or in quick succession. Batching here means managing several state changes that together realize a user operation. Because each transaction consumes a nonce per account, you must manage nonces deliberately, especially when sending many transactions from the same signer. A simple approach is to let the library handle nonces if you await each transaction sequentially. For parallel submissions or batch sending, read the current nonce and increment it for each raw signed transaction you prepare. Another consideration is gas: sending multiple transactions during congested periods increases the risk that some will be delayed or reordered. Consider grouping logically related changes into a single contract call when possible so the EVM executes them atomically and emits predictable events. If separate transactions are necessary, implement robust retry and reconciliation logic in your off-chain service to handle partial failures. A common misconception is that faster submission always wins; network mempools, miners, and EIP-1559 fee dynamics affect ordering. Design with idempotence and eventual consistency in mind. In practical terms, patterns for sending multiple related transactions safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 7.7 › Batching & Nonces
When to batch vs multiple txs
Atomicity, nonce control, and failure handling are the core concerns.
Option A: Single call
Combine related operations into one function so Ethereum executes atomically and emits a single set of events.
Option B: Multiple txs
Send sequential transactions and manage nonces. Add reconciliation logic for partial failures.
Nonce strategy
For parallel sends, fetch current nonce and manually increment when building signed transactions.
// Sequential submission (simple)
await tx1.wait();
await tx2.wait();

// Parallel with manual nonces (advanced)
const nonce = await provider.getTransactionCount(signer.address);
// sign txA with nonce
// sign txB with nonce + 1
Common mistake
Assuming transaction ordering is preserved without managing nonces or fees can lead to unexpected states. Always design for retries and reconciliation.
Why it matters

Correct nonce and gas strategies avoid stuck transactions and inconsistent application state during bursts or network congestion.

screens.title: Gas Price Considerations and EIP-1559
screens.narratorSegment: Gas pricing determines how quickly a transaction is included in a block. Modern networks use EIP-1559 style fee markets where you specify a maxFeePerGas and maxPriorityFeePerGas, rather than a simple gasPrice. ethers. js accepts these fields in the overrides object when sending transactions. For non-critical operations you can rely on library defaults which estimate reasonable values. For time-sensitive operations you may set higher fees to increase miner incentives and speed up inclusion. However, higher fees do not guarantee ordering if nonces and mempool conditions differ. Use gasLimit to avoid out-of-gas reverts and monitor network conditions with a gas tracker during critical windows. A common pitfall is overpaying for routine transactions; another is setting gas values too low and triggering a revert. In scripts, prefer conservative defaults but allow override parameters that can be elevated when an operation is urgent. For batching, remember each transaction's fee compounds the total cost. Always budget for worst-case inclusion fees when coordinating multiple related transactions. Gas Price Considerations and EIP-1559 means use sensible defaults for routine work; override maxfeepergas or maxpriorityfeepergas for urgent transactions while managing overall cost.. Fee selection for critical transactions
EIP-1559 fields let you set a max and priority fee to influence inclusion speed.
// Example override to speed a transaction
await contract.someFunction({
  gasLimit: 200000,
  maxFeePerGas: ethers.utils.parseUnits('100', 'gwei'),
  maxPriorityFeePerGas: ethers.utils.parseUnits('2', 'gwei')
});
  • Default estimators are usually sufficient for normal operations.
  • Raise fees only for time-sensitive transactions to avoid unnecessary costs.
  • Set gasLimit to prevent out-of-gas errors on complex calls.
Common mistake
Using a very large maxFee without understanding the network may lead to unexpectedly high costs; monitor replaced transactions and fee refunds carefully.
Why it matters

Choosing appropriate fees balances speed and cost; it is an operational decision for production dApps.

screens.title: Events vs On-Chain Storage
screens.narratorSegment: It is important to distinguish when to use events and when to write persistent on-chain storage. Events are best for off-chain notification, analytics, and reconstructing user-facing history. They are cheaper than storage writes and optimized for node-side filtering when you index the correct parameters. Storage should be used when on-chain contracts or future transactions need to read and enforce logic based on that data, or when the data is required for protocol invariants. A common example: use events to log user actions for a dashboard, but store balances and ownership in contract state since other contracts may depend on them. A misconception is thinking events can replace storage for logic that must be enforced on-chain. Events cannot be read by contracts and are not part of the contract's persistent state. When designing your contract, ask: does any on-chain code need to consult this data, or is it purely for off-chain visibility? Use events for the latter; use storage for the former. This choice impacts gas, indexing complexity, and the UX of your dApp. Events vs On-Chain Storage means events are for off-chain consumers and cheaper; storage is for on-chain logic and persistence.. Side-by-side comparison
Costs, accessibility, and intended consumers differ.
Events
  • Cheaper than storage for historical logs.
  • Designed for off-chain consumption and filtering.
  • Not accessible to other smart contracts.
Storage
  • Persistent on-chain state readable by contracts.
  • More expensive due to storage gas costs.
  • Required when on-chain logic relies on the data.
Scenario question
You want a transaction history for a user profile page: prefer events. If a future contract must validate a user's historical behavior on-chain: persist verified counters in storage.
Key Takeaway

Choose events for off-chain logs and storage for on-chain verifiable state; design accordingly to balance gas and functionality.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Robust Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize common mistakes and the robust patterns that avoid them. First, failing to index search-relevant fields often leads to expensive client-side filtering; choose up to three fields to index strategically. Second, parsing logs without try-catch makes scripts brittle when receipts contain unrelated logs; always guard parseLog calls. Third, relying on an HTTP provider where you need real-time subscriptions will produce poor results; prefer WebSocket-capable providers for live listeners. Fourth, neglecting gas and nonce management when batching can create stuck or reordered transactions; implement retry and reconciliation logic and consider atomic contract calls when possible. For testing, assert emitted events in unit tests by parsing receipts or using event matchers; don't depend solely on console output. Finally, document which fields are indexed and why so front-end engineers can write correct filters. As a pattern, adopt these four checks on every contract change: index selection, emit placement after state updates, listener/provider compatibility, and receipt parsing with safe error handling. Doing so makes event-driven dApps reliable in development and production. Four common mistakes

  • Parsing logs without handling unknown logs or ABI changes.

Add try-catch around parseLog, choose indexed fields intentionally, use WebSocket providers for listeners, and test events in unit tests by decoding receipts.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore how smart contracts communicate with the off-chain world using events, and why this matters for responsive dApps. Events are structured logs emitted by contracts that off-chain services read efficiently. You will learn the Solidity syntax for defining and emitting events, the role of the indexed keyword for fast filtering, and how listeners in ethers. js subscribe to live events. We will also cover how to extract event data from a transaction receipt after a transaction is mined, and contrast that with live listening. Finally, we examine advanced interaction patterns such as batching multiple actions and consciously setting gas parameters for time-sensitive operations. Throughout the lesson you'll see concrete code examples: a modified Counter contract that emits CountChanged events, a Hardhat listener script that prints events as they arrive, and examples of queryFilter and parseLog usage to retrieve historical events or decode logs. By the end you'll understand when to use events instead of storing history on-chain, how to filter efficiently, and how to handle receipts and gas in real deployments.

By the end of these screens you will be able to name, write, and use Solidity events to connect smart contracts to off-chain systems. You will define events with the correct types, choose which parameters to mark indexed for efficient searching, and use the emit keyword to publish logs. You will also set up listeners with ethers. js, both for continuous updates and for historical queries using filters and queryFilter. Practically, you'll know how to parse transaction receipts and decode raw logs to confirm what a transaction emitted immediately after it is mined. Finally, you will learn advanced on-chain interaction techniques such as batching related transactions with careful nonce handling and choosing appropriate gas parameters for time-sensitive actions. Each objective is designed to give you a concrete capability you can demonstrate with code and a test script.

This second objectives slide focuses on measurable outcomes and practice tasks. You will modify a Counter contract to emit CountChanged events on increment and decrement, redeploy it, and write a Hardhat script that listens and prints structured event data. You will then use queryFilter to reconstruct historical activity for a given block range, and parse a transaction receipt to assert that a specific event was emitted with expected values. You should be able to explain why indexing parameters matters for efficient filtering and identify common mistakes such as not indexing searchable fields or failing to catch parse errors when decoding logs. By completing these tasks you will demonstrate both the Solidity-side and off-chain tooling knowledge needed to make dApps reactive and traceable. Learning Objectives — Practical Outcomes means hands-on tasks let you demonstrate full end-to-end event handling: emit from contract, listen live, query history, and parse receipts to validate behavior.. In practical terms, how you'll prove understanding and apply skills. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's define what a Solidity event is and how to author one correctly. Events are structured logs created by the EVM when a contract executes an emit statement. They are recorded in the transaction receipt and are intended for off-chain consumers, not on-chain logic. In Solidity you declare an event signature with the event keyword followed by parameter types and names. The indexed modifier can mark up to three parameters to be included in the searchable topics array. Indexed parameters make it possible for nodes and clients to filter large sets of logs efficiently, so choosing which fields to index matters in design. For example, a Transfer event often indexes the from and to addresses so dApps can quickly query transfers for a particular account. Keep in mind that indexing moves some data to topics, which affects how you parse logs. Emitting an event is done with emit EventName(args). Emitting costs gas but far less than persisting the same data in storage. A common misconception is that events are accessible to other contracts — they are not; events are for off-chain systems. As you write events, consider which arguments a frontend will want to filter by and mark those indexed. Try creating an event that balances searchability and argument completeness, and then ask: which two or three fields will you index and why?

Now we walk through modifying a simple Counter contract to emit a CountChanged event when the counter moves. The goal is to create a traceable history of user actions with minimal gas. Notice the event signature includes an indexed user address, the newCount, and a short action string to describe increment or decrement. Indexing the user address makes it easy to filter logs by who triggered the change. When writing the increment and decrement functions, increment or decrement the state variable and then emit CountChanged with msg. sender, the updated count, and a descriptive action. Keep the event arguments compact: strings are fine for short descriptors but avoid large blobs. A misconception to avoid is thinking events are part of contract state that other contracts can read — they are off-chain only. After updating the contract, redeploy to a test network and record the address; listeners and queryFilter calls must point at the new address. This simple event pattern is ideal for auditing user interactions, powering UI updates, and offloading historical data from storage. Modify Counter.sol to emit CountChanged means emit concise, searchable events that capture who acted and what changed; index the identity fields you will query.. In practical terms, practical solidity edit and reasoning behind the event design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Next we'll examine a Node/Hardhat script that subscribes to CountChanged events and prints human-friendly messages to the terminal. This pattern is common for backend services, logs, or local development where you want immediate feedback. The script attaches to a deployed contract by address and uses contract. on with the event name. The callback receives event arguments followed by an event object that contains the transaction hash and block number. Notice the example awaits nothing after attaching — the script keeps running to listen for new events. In production you will integrate graceful shutdown, error handling, and possibly a process manager. A common oversight is failing to attach the contract with a provider that supports websockets or polling; some providers require WebSocket endpoints for continuous subscriptions. It is important to distinguish when to use events and when to write persistent on-chain storage. Events are best for off-chain notification, analytics, and reconstructing user-facing history. They are cheaper than storage writes and optimized for node-side filtering when you index the correct parameters. Storage should be used when on-chain contracts or future transactions need to read and enforce logic based on that data, or when the data is required for protocol invariants. A common example: use events to log user actions for a dashboard, but store balances and ownership in contract state since other contracts may depend on them. Let's summarize common mistakes and the robust patterns that avoid them. First, failing to index search-relevant fields often leads to expensive client-side filtering; choose up to three fields to index strategically. Second, parsing logs without try-catch makes scripts brittle when receipts contain unrelated logs; always guard parseLog calls. Third, relying on an HTTP provider where you need real-time subscriptions will produce poor results; prefer WebSocket-capable providers for live listeners. Fourth, neglecting gas and nonce management when batching can create stuck or reordered transactions; implement retry and reconciliation logic and consider atomic contract calls when possible. For testing, assert emitted events in unit tests by parsing receipts or using event matchers; don't depend solely on console output. Finally, document which fields are indexed and why so front-end engineers can write correct filters.
